newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai parties reject national government proposal.
newsitem.headline: Thai parties reject national government proposal.

text.p: Major Thai political parties on Thursday rejected a proposal from university lecturers for Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh to dissolve his coalition in favour of a new broader government to tackle the country's economic crisis.

The collapse of Thailand's property sector and turmoil in its financial sector have forced the government to seek financial assistance from the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Its economy is growing at its slowest rate in several decades.
Lecturers representing four universities met and sought support of their proposal from former Prime Minister and privy counsellor Prem Tinsulanonda.

"We are urging politicians to set aside differences by dissolving (Chavalit's) ruling coalition and forming a national government comprising the four major parties before some undemocratic power steps in," Theeraphat Serirangsan, leader of the academic group, told reporters after meeting Prem.
Theeraphat referred to recent rumours that the military may take advantage of current economic problems and stage a coup against Chavalit.

The university lecturers called for Chavalit's New Aspiration Party (NAP) to merge with his coalition partner Chart Pattana Party, the opposition Democrat Party of former premier Chuan Leekpai, and opposition Chart Thai Party of former Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa.
The Thai armed forces, which staged 17 coups or attempted coups since 1932 when the country switched from absolute monarchy to a parliamentary system, have denied they planned to stage an overthrow.
Prem, a premier for eight years in the 1980s, enjoys high public respect and his advice is widely heeded by most generals and politicians.
Opposition leader Chuan of the Democrat party turned down the proposal. "I am confident the current system works. One should not rush to accept the national government proposal."

Chuan, whose Democrat Party won 123 parliamentary seats in the last general election in late 1996, two less than Chavalit's NAP, conceded that Thailand faced grave economic problems but he said any government change should take place within the framework of the parliamentary system.
"The prime minister should resign and allow parliament to nominate a successor to form a new coaliton," Democrat spokesman Abhisit Vejjajiva told Reuters.

Another opposition party echoed Chuan's opinion. "Everyone is aware that the ruling coalition faces a political and economic crisis and it has totally lost public faith. But the Chart Thai Party believes a national government is not needed at this stage," Chart Thai spokesman Somsak Prisana-anantakul said.
Chavalit's six-party coalition controls 222 seats in the 393-member elected House of Representatives. It last week decided to seek an international loan package sponsored by the IMF.
The prime minister hinted early this week of possible changes of his cabinet after Thailand signed the IMF rescue package later this month.
"The Prime minister has hinted that after August 21, there will be changes but I don't have any details," government spokesman Varathep Rattanakorn told Reuters. REUTER SUT VA
